transcript.text: My Hotpoint washer dryer isn't drying properly any more and there's a funny smell when it's on the dry bit. Is there something I should clean?

Yes, cleaning is very likely the answer here. Poor drying together with a funny smell only on the dry part is most often fluff. Drying throws off a lot of lint, and when it builds up it blocks the airflow, so the clothes stay damp. Less likely causes are drying too big a load or using a short or low dryness setting. The heater side (element, thermostat or a tripped cut-out) comes after that, and even a tripped cut-out is usually caused by the same fluff build-up. If the smell is ever strong or smoky, stop the cycle, unplug it and let it cool before doing anything else. 1. Lint or fluff filter. Some washer-dryers have a fluff filter for the drying air, often near the door seal or behind a small cover. Your manual will show whether yours has one. If it does, take it out and clean off all the fluff. If it was matted, that alone could explain both the poor drying and the smell. 2. Pump filter (bottom front, behind a small flap). On many washer-dryers the drying fluff ends up here, and a clogged filter stops the condensed water getting away. Unplug the machine, put towels down and have a shallow tray ready, because water will come out. Unscrew the filter slowly, clear the fluff and screw it back firmly. A lot of fluff here means you've probably found the culprit. 3. Water supply and drain. Most washer-dryers use a trickle of cold water to condense the moisture while drying. Make sure the cold tap is fully on and that the fill and drain hoses behind the machine aren't kinked or squashed. A restriction here leaves clothes hot but damp. 4. Load and setting. A washer-dryer only dries roughly half what it washes (for example an 8 kg wash might be about 5 kg dry). Try a smaller dry load on a full drying programme. Also check the clothes come out of the spin damp rather than dripping. If they're wet going into the dry, the problem is the spin or drain, not the drying. If it dries well and the smell goes after that, it was the fluff. To help me narrow it down if not: during drying, does it get properly hot but leave things damp, or does it stay cool with no real heat? Roughly how big a load were you drying? It gets really hot, the top of the machine feels very hot to touch, but the clothes stay damp. I usually dry a full wash load, about 8-9kg. The smell is like burning dust or scorched fabric, and I've kept using it for the last few cycles.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A very hot machine with damp clothes means the heater is working, but the hot, moist air isn't moving through and condensing as it should. A burning-dust or scorched-fabric smell is a common sign of fluff cooking on the hot drying element because of that restricted airflow. Please stop using the drying function, and the machine as a whole, until a qualified engineer has checked it. A burning smell over several cycles means something inside may already be scorched, so this has gone beyond a simple clean. 1. Fluff build-up in the drying air path. This blocks the airflow, so heat builds up (hence the very hot top) and lint scorches on the element. A blocked internal air duct or condenser can't be cleared without dismantling the machine, which is engineer work.
2. Drying too big a load. An 8-9kg load is probably well over what it can dry. Most washer-dryers of that size dry roughly 5-6kg. An overfull drum dries poorly and sheds more lint, so it feeds cause 1.
3. The condensing water supply not keeping up. This would also give you hot but damp clothes.
4. Less likely, the drying thermostat or cut-out isn't controlling the heat properly. The strength of the heat on the top makes it worth an engineer checking. 1. If they're packed with fluff, that points to an airflow blockage inside as well. If they're clean, the engineer will look harder at the internal duct, the condenser and the thermostat.
2. Find the dry capacity on the door rim, front panel or in the manual, so you know the right dry load for the future. Splitting a full wash into two dry loads is normal for a washer-dryer.
3. Note anything you see, such as brown or singed fluff or scorch marks, and tell the engineer. It's also worth putting your model number into Hotpoint's own safety and recall checker, and having a look at GOV.UK product safety alerts. I can't say whether yours is affected, but it only takes a minute. As for repair or replace: if it turns out to be a fluff blockage plus maybe a cut-out or thermostat, that's usually a reasonable repair. If the element or wiring has been badly scorched on an older machine, it's worth asking the engineer

candidates: Fluff build-up restricting airflow (lint filter, pump filter or condenser path), with fluff scorching on the drying elem (high)
Dry load too big for the dry capacity, a short or low dryness setting, or the cold water supply for condensing being off (medium)
Drying heater element, its thermostat or a tripped thermal cut-out (often caused by the airflow restriction) (low)
